Policy stance and outlook: The FOMC kept the federal funds rate at 0–0.25% and continued QE (at least $80B Treasuries and $40B agency MBS per month), consistent with average inflation targeting that allows inflation to moderately exceed 2% for a time to anchor expectations. Administered rates (IORB at 0.15%, ON RRP at 0.05%, ON repo at 0.25%) and forward guidance aim to keep financial conditions accommodative while the Committee monitors progress toward maximum employment and sustained 2% inflation.

SLOOS cross-check (July 2021) tilts conditions more constructive:
- Banks reported stronger demand for C&I loans across large, middle‑market, and small firms, alongside higher borrower inquiries; many banks eased C&I terms. Foreign banks also reported stronger C&I demand, driven by financing needs for inventories, accounts receivable, capex, and M&A, with terms largely unchanged.
- Consumer credit conditions loosened: banks eased standards for credit card, auto, and other consumer loans.
- Residential real estate lending saw easing across several mortgage categories (with GSE-eligible largely unchanged); demand for Qualified Mortgage loans strengthened; subprime originations remained limited.
- Commercial real estate showed some easing, notably in multifamily.
- Reasons cited for easing included improved economic outlook, competition, risk appetite, liquidity, and capital position.

Implications: The broad-based strengthening in loan demand and easing of bank lending standards suggest the bank credit channel is reinforcing the Fed’s accommodative policy, supporting the recovery and transmission to households and businesses. While the Financial Stability Report flags elevated vulnerabilities (stretched valuations, nonbank fragilities, select CRE pockets), the SLOOS backdrop modestly improves the near-term growth and credit availability narrative versus a purely cautious read.
